name: Volt Falls
description:
The falls still fall. That much hasn't changed. 750,000 gallons per second pouring over a 50-meter cliff face, generating enough hydroelectric power to light a city — which is exactly what they do, though the city they light bears no resemblance to the tourist trap that existed a century ago. The observation decks are still there, maintained by Mirrorwell Media as an 'experiential heritage installation,' which means you can still watch the water if you pay the admission fee. Most people don't. The power is worth more than the view.

Volt Falls is the GLMZ's primary clean energy node on the Canadian side. Ouroboros Energy holds sovereign authority over the generating facilities — a complex of turbine halls, transformer stations, and distribution infrastructure that extends for 12 kilometers along the Niagara River gorge. The old tourist district — wax museums, haunted houses, chain restaurants — has been partially demolished, partially repurposed, and entirely absorbed into the energy infrastructure's support economy. Casino towers that once drew gamblers from Toronto now house Ouroboros administrative staff and the engineers who keep the turbines turning. The irony is perfect: the city that sold spectacle now sells watts, and the watts are more honest.

The border with the American side runs down the middle of the river, and the energy generated by the falls is split between Canadian and American grids by treaty — the Niagara Power Allocation Protocol, renegotiated every five years with increasing hostility. The American side, controlled by Cinderfall Energy, consistently pushes for a larger share. The Canadian side, controlled by Ouroboros, consistently resists. The falls don't care. They generate power regardless of who claims it, which is the most politically neutral statement anyone has made about Niagara in decades. Below the generating facilities, the gorge itself has become a restricted zone — the infrastructure is too valuable to allow public access, and the security perimeter extends to the water's edge.

sights: The falls themselves — still magnificent, now framed by turbine intake structures and power distribution arrays
Ouroboros transformer stations lining the gorge, humming with visible electrical discharge
The old casino towers repurposed as corporate housing, their neon signs replaced with Ouroboros branding
Power distribution lines radiating outward from the falls like a spider's web made of copper and ambition
The American side visible across the gorge, Cinderfall's competing infrastructure mirroring Ouroboros's
sounds: The falls — a constant roar that you stop hearing and start feeling, a vibration in every surface
Turbine harmonics — a deep, mechanical chord underlying the water's thunder
Transformer hum at frequencies that make your augments twitch if they're not properly shielded
The absence of tourist noise — the loudest natural wonder in the GLMZ, surrounded by industrial silence
smells: Ozone from the generating facilities — clean, sharp, electric
Mist from the falls, carrying the mineral tang of the Great Lakes
Transformer coolant — a faint, sweet chemical note
atmosphere.feel: A place where nature's indifference to human ambition is converted into kilowatt-hours. The falls are sublime. The infrastructure is mundane. The combination is Volt Falls — the most beautiful power plant in the world, and a power plant all the same.

demographics: Population 320,000, predominantly Ouroboros employees and their dependents. The engineering corps — turbine specialists, grid management technicians, power distribution experts — forms a technical aristocracy. Service workers who support the infrastructure and its people make up the Tier 1 and 2 base. Tourists are technically still welcome. Tourists rarely come.
economy: Hydroelectric power generation and distribution. Ouroboros Energy's Niagara operations supply approximately 15% of the Canadian GLMZ's electricity. The tourism economy that sustained the old city is effectively dead, replaced by the support economy for 320,000 energy workers. Mirrorwell Media maintains the heritage installations as a tax write-off.
power_structure: Ouroboros Energy sovereign territory, with minimal Canadian federal oversight limited to the Niagara Power Allocation Protocol negotiations. The generating facilities are classified as critical infrastructure, which grants Ouroboros expanded security authority. The municipal government exists to maintain residential zones outside the energy infrastructure perimeter.
dangers: Power infrastructure sabotage — the generating facilities are the highest-value target on the Canadian lakeshore
Transformer field exposure — the electromagnetic environment near the facilities affects unshielded augmentations
The Niagara Power Allocation Protocol negotiations turning violent — it's happened twice in the last decade
The gorge restricted zone — trespass is met with automated defense systems
Ouroboros security operating under critical infrastructure authority — expanded powers, limited accountability
opportunities: Energy sector expertise is the most portable skill in the GLMZ — Volt Falls-trained engineers are recruited globally
Power allocation intelligence is valuable to both Ouroboros and Cinderfall
The old tourist infrastructure contains pre-corporate spaces that Ouroboros hasn't mapped or secured
The border dispute creates demand for negotiators, intermediaries, and people who can work both sides
story_hooks: Ouroboros is diverting a percentage of generating capacity to an unlisted facility beneath the gorge — the power goes in, nothing comes out, and the energy budget doesn't balance
The Niagara Power Allocation Protocol is up for renegotiation, and someone is assassinating the negotiators on both sides
The falls' output has increased by 3% over the last year — more water, more power — and nobody can explain where the additional water is coming from
